transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I’m here because things at work have gotten… not normal. I do mathematical modeling, environmental datasets, contract work, and there’s this project where I’m supposed to be leading the revisions. And I know people keep saying it’s just version-control problems, you know, files getting overwritten or someone using an older copy, but it’s more patterned than that.

It looks to me like the people on that environmental modeling contract are tracking my revisions. I’ll make changes, careful changes, and then errors show up in the datasets later—errors I know I didn’t put there. And they’re the kind of mistakes that make me look sloppy, like I can’t manage the work or shouldn’t be leading it. My wife says I’m reading too much into it, and a couple of the junior analysts act like it’s just normal confusion with shared files, but… I’ve done this kind of work a long time. I know what ordinary mistakes look like. This feels planted.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is there?

Voices? I mean… no, not in the way people usually mean that, I don’t think. I’m not sitting in a room hearing someone talking to me when nobody’s there. At least, I haven’t noticed anything like that.

Sometimes I’ll replay conversations in my head, especially work conversations, like what someone said in a meeting or how they said it, and I can get pretty stuck on that. But that’s more like thinking through it, not a voice coming from outside me. So… no, I wouldn’t say I’m hearing voices.
Have you been feeling unusually energized or high lately?

Unusually energized or high? No, I don’t think so. Not “high,” anyway. I haven’t been walking around feeling euphoric or like I have limitless energy, if that’s what you mean.

I mean, I can get keyed up when I’m trying to sort something out, especially if there’s a deadline or if something in the work doesn’t add up. Then I’ll keep turning it over in my head because I don’t like leaving a problem unresolved. But that’s not the same as feeling great or energized in some unusual way. It feels more like… pressure, or being on alert. So no, I wouldn’t say I’ve been unusually energized.
Do ordinary things around you ever seem to carry a special message meant specifically for you?

I don’t know if I’d put it exactly like “ordinary things” sending me messages. It’s not like the television is talking to me or road signs are giving me instructions or anything like that.

But with the work files, yes, there are things that feel very specifically aimed at me. Like when I make revisions on the environmental modeling contract, and then later errors appear in the datasets—errors that are just the kind that would make me look incompetent as the lead. To someone else, maybe it looks like a normal version-control issue, someone used the wrong file or overwrote something. My wife says that, and the junior analysts say that too. But the pattern is too consistent.

It feels like those mistakes are not random. They’re placed there to send a message, I guess—not in words, but to show me that people are tracking what I’m changing and can interfere with it. And also to make other people think I can’t handle the project. So… not special messages from objects, no. But the changes in the datasets, the timing of them, the way they show up after I’ve touched the work—that feels meant for me.
If someone showed you clear proof that these file errors were just routine version-control mistakes, would you still believe people were deliberately trying to undermine you?

If someone showed me clear proof… I mean, I’d have to look at what you mean by “clear,” because that’s the problem. People keep saying “version-control mistakes” like that explains everything, but it doesn’t explain the timing, or why the errors show up right after I’ve made revisions, or why they’re the kind of errors that make me look like I don’t know what I’m doing.

If there was real proof, not just someone saying, “Oh, this happens all the time,” I’d consider it. I’m not trying to be unreasonable. I have a math background, I understand mistakes happen in files and datasets. But this has felt too consistent to just wave away. My wife says I’m reading too much into it, and the junior analysts say it’s probably routine file confusion, but from where I’m sitting it looks like people on that contract are tracking my changes and planting problems so I’ll take the blame.

So… would I still believe it? I think I’d still be suspicious, yes. Maybe I’d question it a little if the proof was really solid, but I don’t think one explanation would erase the whole pattern for me.
Have you been feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed most of the day nearly every day… I’m not sure I’d say that. I mean, I’ve had times where I feel worn down or frustrated, especially when things feel like they’re not going right, but “depressed” sounds like a very specific thing, like feeling low all day, day after day.

I don’t think I’ve noticed that in myself in that way. I can get discouraged, sure, and I can spend a lot of time thinking about things, but I wouldn’t say I’m sad or depressed most of the day nearly every day. At least not that I’d describe it that way.
Did this sense that people are tracking your work and trying to undermine you start recently, or have you tended to feel this way about people for much of your adult life?

No, I wouldn’t say it’s been my whole adult life. I mean, I’ve always been careful with my work, maybe more careful than some people, because in math and modeling a small error can make you look bad even if the rest of the work is solid. But this particular sense—that people on this project are watching my revisions and then errors are showing up afterward, like they’re being placed there—has really been more recent.

I’d say about the last two months. That’s when it started feeling less like ordinary sloppiness or file confusion and more like a pattern aimed at me. Before that, I might have been irritated by mistakes or office politics like anyone else, but I wasn’t walking around thinking people were tracking my work this way. It’s really this project, and the last couple of months, where it became hard to ignore.
Has this belief that people are deliberately altering your work been present continuously for at least one month?

Yes. I mean, if you’re asking whether it’s just been a passing thought for a few days, then no—it’s been there longer than that. The feeling that people on the project are watching my revisions and then deliberately putting errors in, that’s been going on for about the last two months.

It hasn’t been, you know, every single second of every day in the sense that I can’t think about anything else, but the belief itself hasn’t really gone away. Once I started seeing that pattern, it’s been hard to unsee it. So yes, definitely more than a month.
Have you become much less emotionally expressive lately—for example, do people say your face or voice seems flat?

I don’t know if I’d describe it exactly as my face or voice being flat. People don’t usually say it to me that way, at least not directly. But I have noticed that I’m… less responsive, I guess. Less animated.

These days I can sit for hours at my desk, or out in the garage, and the telescope will still be covered. I know I used to like using it. I used to go to those astronomy nights, talk with people about equipment or what we were looking at, and it wasn’t a chore. Same with hiking, or even mentoring the younger analysts at work—I used to get something out of explaining a problem or helping someone see the structure of it.

Now I’ll think, “I should do that,” or “I used to care about that,” but there’s just not much pull to start. And talking to people feels like it takes more effort than it should. So maybe that comes across as flat. I’m not trying to be cold or anything. It’s more like things don’t get enough traction inside me to show on the outside.
Compared with a few months ago, has your ability to do your job gotten noticeably worse?

Yes… yes, it has. I don’t like saying that, because my work has always been the one area where I felt pretty competent, but compared with a few months ago I’m not keeping up the way I used to.

I’ve fallen behind on the modeling deliverables—far enough that it wasn’t just me staying late to catch up or asking for an extra day. The firm had to reassign pieces of the contract to other people. That’s embarrassing. And it’s not just the technical work itself; I’m supposed to be supervising some of the junior analysts, helping them think through assumptions and check their approach, and lately I’m not much use to them. I either don’t respond quickly, or I get stuck in the weeds and can’t give them the kind of clear guidance I used to.

At home it’s similar, I guess. I mostly keep to myself, and my wife has to push me to keep basic routines going—getting moving, taking care of ordinary things. So, yes, noticeably worse. Not completely unable to work, but definitely not functioning at the level I was.
Have other people told you lately that your speech is hard to follow or that you jump from one idea to another in a way that doesn’t make sense to them?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t think people have said it in exactly those words, like “you’re hard to follow” or “you’re jumping around.” At least, not that I remember.

Sometimes my wife will ask me to slow down or explain what I mean, but that could just be because I’m giving too much context. I’ve always had a tendency to do that—if I’m explaining a work problem, I want to start with the assumptions, then the model, then why one change affects another thing. So I don’t always know whether someone is confused because I’m actually not making sense, or because I’m taking the long way around.

At work, people have seemed impatient with me lately, or they’ll sort of steer the conversation back to the main point. But I don’t know that anyone has directly told me my speech doesn’t make sense. I haven’t noticed myself suddenly switching topics for no reason, if that’s what you mean. I may go into too much detail, but in my mind there’s usually a connection.
Have these problems overall been going on for six months or more?

Yes. It’s definitely been more than six months.

If I try to put a real starting point on it, I’d say the whole decline started after I was put in charge of that larger environmental modeling contract… that was about two years and two months ago now. At first I kept telling myself it was just the pressure of the project, or that I was adjusting to the responsibility, because it was a bigger scope than what I’d handled before. But looking back, that’s when things began shifting, and it hasn’t really gone back to normal since then.

So, yes—this isn’t just a few bad weeks or even a rough season. It’s been going on for quite a while.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been disorganized speech/thought disorder, which would support schizophrenia over acute polymorphic psychotic disorder with schizophrenic symptoms.
doctor.question: Have other people told you lately that your speech is hard to follow or that you jump from one idea to another in a way that doesn’t make sense to them?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about disorganized speech or thought process, such as being hard to follow or jumping between ideas. The provided symptom profile does not include a specific item for disorganized speech, so no listed item directly applies.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t think people have said it in exactly those words, like “you’re hard to follow” or “you’re jumping around.” At least, not that I remember.

Sometimes my wife will ask me to slow down or explain what I mean, but that could just be because I’m giving too much context. I’ve always had a tendency to do that—if I’m explaining a work problem, I want to start with the assumptions, then the model, then why one change affects another thing. So I don’t always know whether someone is confused because I’m actually not making sense, or because I’m taking the long way around.

At work, people have seemed impatient with me lately, or they’ll sort of steer the conversation back to the main point. But I don’t know that anyone has directly told me my speech doesn’t make sense. I haven’t noticed myself suddenly switching topics for no reason, if that’s what you mean. I may go into too much detail, but in my mind there’s usually a connection.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the total duration of psychotic symptoms has reached six months, which best distinguishes schizophrenia from acute polymorphic psychotic disorder with schizophrenic symptoms.
doctor.question: Have these problems overall been going on for six months or more?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This whole decline started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract about two years and two months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the overall problems have been going on, specifically whether the duration is six months or more.

patient.answer:
Yes. It’s definitely been more than six months.

If I try to put a real starting point on it, I’d say the whole decline started after I was put in charge of that larger environmental modeling contract… that was about two years and two months ago now. At first I kept telling myself it was just the pressure of the project, or that I was adjusting to the responsibility, because it was a bigger scope than what I’d handled before. But looking back, that’s when things began shifting, and it hasn’t really gone back to normal since then.

So, yes—this isn’t just a few bad weeks or even a rough season. It’s been going on for quite a while.

inference.note: Duration >6 months with functional decline and negative symptoms narrows away from acute/transient psychotic disorder (F23.3) and supports schizophrenia, paranoid subtype (F20.0).

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a persistent persecutory delusion that coworkers are tracking his revisions and planting errors to undermine him, present continuously for about two months. There is also clear functional decline over a much longer period, with negative symptoms such as reduced motivation, social withdrawal, and diminished emotional responsiveness. The overall disturbance has lasted well over six months, while mood episodes and hallucinations were denied. This pattern is most consistent with paranoid schizophrenia.
